connect claude code and codex # connect claude code and codex

shield setup registers native hooks and mcp tools for a project. hooks check
supported tool requests; mcp lets the agent inspect policy and propose changes.
for your first installation, follow [the setup guide](getting-started.md).

## which part does what?

| part | what you use it for |
| --- | --- |
| native hooks | check supported requests from the agent's ordinary tools against active policy. |
| shield mcp tools | let the agent inspect policy, read guides, evaluate diagnostic requests, and prepare reviewed changes. |
| operator cli | initialize the project and confirm settings or policy changes yourself. |

after setup, restart and trust the agent so it loads both integrations.
use `shield history list` to inspect recorded requests and completion.

## install or repair an integration

initialize the project with `shield init`, then run `shield mcp setup --agent claude` in an operator terminal to install native
command hooks and shield's project mcp entry. confirmation shows the owned files,
binary and project. claude uses `.claude/settings.local.json` and `.mcp.json`.
to add codex as well, run `shield mcp setup --agent codex`; codex uses
`.codex/hooks.json` and `.codex/config.toml`. no user/global settings are changed.
when active rules ask for [codex prefix rules](policy-rules.md#codex-prefix-rules),
shield also writes `.codex/rules/shield.rules`. setup and every activation rewrite
it, removing it when no such rule remains or codex is removed. codex loads it
only for a trusted project. shield never replaces a file at that path that it
did not write; status and the activation receipt say to move such a file aside.
status also reports a stale file and hand edits, and `shield mcp setup`
repairs them. until then, codex asks block whatever the ask fallback, because
the file may let codex skip its sandbox. setup and policy reviews list the
prefixes a change adds or removes.

other hook groups, mcp servers, plugins, settings and codex rules files survive
installation and removal. repeating setup creates one registration per agent.
missing entries can be repaired by selecting the agent again. edited owned
entries conflict; shield preserves them and requires resolution. `shield mcp setup`
without `--agent` resumes a confirmed interrupted plan. `shield mcp setup --remove`
removes the agents you select, and with every agent selected removes all owned
registrations while preserving policy, approvals and history.

## load the hooks

restart the agent, trust the project, enable hooks, and approve the mcp
connection. in codex, review hook definitions through `/hooks`. shield cannot
override host trust or administrator restrictions.

setup's tool permissions page marks tools that can run without prompting.
all except `policy_apply` are marked by default; later setup preserves
your choices. codex uses a `prompt` server setting with `approve` for marked
tools. claude adds `mcp__shield__<tool>` entries to `permissions.allow` and
`shield` to `enabledmcpjsonservers` in `.claude/settings.local.json`.

mcp policy changes need separate approval. claude opens a confirmation form:
accept applies, while decline or cancel leaves the proposal pending. the form
works in `default`, `auto`, and `bypasspermissions` modes, independently of
ordinary tool approval. clients without form elicitation cannot apply.
codex uses its tool approval prompt; `never` approval policy refuses apply.
see [mcp review](project-mcp.md#proposals-and-operator-review).

repeating setup repairs missing tool approvals. unmarking a tool or removing
shield deletes only approvals shield added; other servers and existing approvals
are preserved. check `shield doctor --json` for missing or changed files and
binaries. status reports live verification as `unverified`.

## intercepted requests

pretooluse checks requests against the registered project's policy.

| request | check |
| --- | --- |
| claude read | file read. |
| claude write, edit, multiedit, notebookedit | file write. |
| claude glob, grep | read of the search path. |
| claude bash and monitor commands | shell policy. |
| codex `view_image` | image-file read; calls naming another environment block. |
| codex `webrun` searches and direct url opens | web policy, as described below. |
| bound project mcp tool calls | mcp policy using the stable project connection id and full arguments. |

configure these bindings through [project mcp connections](mcp-connections.md).
unbound servers retain their host behavior. bound calls whose project settings
drift are blocked until setup is reviewed again. codex's inner mcp calls from
code mode use the same per-call hook path.

session-management tools pass through to the host's permissions. for claude,
these include tool loading, task lists and stopping tasks, questions, plan mode,
scheduling, subagents, workflows, agent listing, skills, and mcp resource listing.
invoked tools are checked normally, except in remotely running subagents or
workflows. codex passes through plans, questions, permission requests, tool search,
timing, subagents, and mcp resource listing.

unsupported tools ask in claude and block in codex. examples include mcp resource
reads; claude also asks for session messages, worktrees, lsp, powershell, and
artifacts. tool messages name supported alternatives where available. a rule
cannot add support for an unmodeled tool.

### web requests

codex `webrun` supports `search_query` and `open` with direct http(s) urls,
including mixed batches of up to 16 operations. every operation must pass.
an optional `lineno` only positions the view. opaque result references, clicks,
and other actions block the entire call. submit a direct url when available.
the hook sees the initial url, not later redirect destinations.

### protected files and policy changes

claude can read and commit `.shield/config.yml`, `rules.yml`, and `shield.lock`,
but cannot edit them or read `.shield/review/`. reading agent settings or
`.mcp.json` asks because they may hold credentials. `.shield/.gitignore` excludes
private review state and cache files. change configurable protection with
[`shield protection set`](project-review.md#protected-files).

agents cannot run shield's operator cli. they inspect policy through mcp,
prepare proposals, and submit `policy_apply` with the returned
`apply_arguments`. you can also review proposals with `shield policy review`.
a proposal changes no permissions until accepted.

the first relevant ask supplies candidate pack/rule guidance and a proposal
route separately from the user-facing permission message. ordinary allowed
claude requests and shield mcp hook checks add no extra model context.
for project scripts, inspect definitions, lifecycle hooks, and arguments before
proposing a rule.

shell denials name up to three denied command forms and their matching rule ids
when that evidence is available. inspect those rules with `rule_list` before
proposing an allowance. a command can be denied for its argument form even when
its input file is readable; folder-access suggestions require a matching
outside-location failure.

claude ask reads and shell requests use its permission prompt or sdk callback;
without a permission host, they block. stored grants belong to the separate
[sdk consumer](claude-read-only.md) and cannot authorize native-hook retries.
arguments containing only an unresolved exit-status expansion (`$?` or `${?}`),
such as `echo "exit $?"`, keep ordinary approval instead of requiring a rewrite.
shield does not guess the status or propose exact literal arguments for it.
explicit command denials still block these requests; other unresolved expansions
retain their existing rewrite requirements.

### file reads

read-only text filters can use file-read policy when their only command match is
a yielding fallback or no rule matches. the supported `jq` forms include string
interpolation, arrays and objects (including shorthand fields such as
`{id, decision}`), slices, selections, regular-expression tests and output formats
such as `@tsv`. environment access, module loading, extra-input
helpers and file-loading options keep ordinary command review. explicit command
ask/deny rules retain precedence.
pagers such as `less` and `more` require command approval or a command rule;
permission to read their input files does not authorize their execution.

### temporary and session files

claude and codex native adapters include the system temporary folders in the
read/write location unions. on unix this includes existing `/tmp` and `/var/tmp`
roots plus the native per-user temporary directory; macos aliases resolve to
their actual directories. existing and newly created temporary files need no
folder proposal or session ownership check. explicit command/rule denials and
protected shield files still apply. removing or replacing a temporary root
itself is blocked. this access does not edit project `access_paths`.

temporary environment overrides do not open the home directory, its ancestors
or its descendants, including `.ssh`, `.claude` and `.codex`. shield checks the
resolved directory, so a symlink alias cannot bypass that boundary. custom
scratch under home follows ordinary project access or an explicitly reviewed
`access_paths` grant.

for claude native hooks, the read union also includes the current session's
`tool-results` directory when its transcript path matches the registered project,
session id and configured claude directory. this allows inspection of persisted
tool output through read or supported text filters. outside temporary folders,
other sessions, settings, credentials and writes receive no extra access through
this session scope. directory or operand symlinks
cannot redirect this scope outside the verified artifact directory. the scope is
observed afresh for each callback and is unavailable to mcp diagnostic input.

status lists supported working-file categories. runtime assets and scratch
folders outside temporary roots are not automatically discovered.

### shell analysis

bash source retains flags, quoting and compounds for conservative shell analysis.
a literal `cd` to the already known current directory, including `cd .`, keeps
that working-directory context and needs no extra approval unless an explicit
command rule asks or denies it. other directory changes retain conservative
handling; returning to the original path after an unresolved change does not
restore known context.
heredocs and here-strings supply inline data without an extra approval requirement.
the command, output destinations, substitutions and shell interpreter bodies
still follow their own policy checks, so writing a quoted heredoc to an approved
project file can proceed when both the command and write are allowed.
standalone `[` and `]` in tests such as
`if [ -f agents.md ]; then cat agents.md; fi` preserve the working-directory
evidence for the read. shield checks every branch against policy; an existence
test does not authorize the read or skip checks on a missing file.
codex permitted requests return brief model context without an explicit allow
response or argument rewrite; ask fallback retains the original policy decision.
exact shell rules match the complete supplied vendor input and available context.
protected-path checks resolve existing symlink targets, including ancestors of new files.
agent shell tools cannot launch shield's operator cli or its literal
`mcp serve` startup sequence under another executable name. use the registered
shield mcp tools to propose changes and request approval.
allow permits the command; deny blocks it. unmatched requests ask. when the only
explanation for an ask is source shield cannot inspect, such as `$(…)`, `eval` or
`sh -c`, the hook blocks the request and tells the agent which part to rewrite as
literal, separate commands; the rewritten request then gets its actual decision.
### codex approval handling

codex pretooluse cannot request native approval. setup preserves a saved fallback
or defaults a new choice to **allow** for every profile, including strict. the
final review shows it without a separate picker. allow includes unmatched
commands and explicit ask rules; deny, unsupported tools and protection failures
still block, and so does an ask on a command a shield prefix rule covers, which
codex would run outside its sandbox without asking. repeating `shield mcp setup --agent codex`
preserves a saved block or allow choice. history retains
policy ask and the configured handoff, without recording individual approval.
automatic ask allowance is suspended while a confirmed setup plan needs repair;
run `shield mcp setup` to finish that plan.

codex also installs permissionrequest for approvals codex independently raises.
shield evaluates the request again against current policy. deny blocks; ask
returns no decision, leaving codex's approval flow in control. policy allow can
resolve the approval using the available host context. an explicit workdir takes
precedence; otherwise shield uses codex's reported session cwd for all supported
commands. missing workdir or tool ids do not change policy allow into ask.
fresh policy allow approves without a prompt or codex rules file; ask and deny
still apply. history records missing execution context as incomplete while
retaining the policy decision and its actual handoff. the reported session cwd
is the evaluation context, not proof of a hidden per-command execution directory.
with the blocking fallback, an ask stopped at pretooluse never reaches this event.
neither abstention nor completion establishes that a person approved a request.

`node --check file` and `node -c file` are syntax checks, with an optional `--`
before the single filename. this applies to bare `node`, `/bin/node` and
`/usr/bin/node`; other executable paths follow ordinary command policy.
when node has no specific rule beyond a yielding ask
fallback, shield decides the check through file-read policy. an ordinary readable
project source can therefore pass without an ask fallback or a node permission
pack. explicit command ask/deny rules, outside-folder rules and protected files
still apply. extra runtime flags, stdin and multiple filenames retain ordinary
command evaluation.
when supplied environment metadata contains node preload options in `node_options`
(`--require`/`-r`, `--import`, `--loader` or `--experimental-loader`), shell syntax
checks also retain execution review because startup code can run.

submitted relative paths use known request cwd. after a cwd change the analyzer
cannot resolve, relative file redirections and supported destructive file operations
block because shield cannot verify their targets. ordinary file moves into the
project root follow policy; replacing or moving protected configuration blocks.
redirections to `/dev/null` and between numbered descriptors, such as
`2>/dev/null` or `2>&1`, open no project file and need no policy.

finite literal `for` loops check their commands through normal policy lookup.
a supported loop and its resolved `break` or `continue` do not require approval
on their own; an explicit policy restriction still applies. for example, if
`node src/server.js` needs approval inside a loop, shield names that invocation.
unresolved command arguments or unsupported control flow can separately require
a rewrite or approval.
using `path` as the loop variable separately asks because it changes which
executables the commands select.

for a simple background command such as `node src/server.js &`, shield tracks
the runtime pid's origin through `$!`, `pid=$!`, and whole-variable copies such
as `copy="$pid"`. a supported `kill "$copy"` can therefore reach the normal
ask flow instead of requiring a rewrite for an unknown operand. known ifs must
preserve a single numeric field for unquoted targets; quoting avoids splitting.
overwrites, uncertain branch values, unsupported mutations, arithmetic, indirect
references and values read from files do not establish this provenance.
only positive pid references with supported literal signal options are modeled;
process-group and name-based targets retain ordinary evaluation.
the pid remains symbolic: shield does not know its number or verify that the
original process is still alive. this analysis never grants policy allow for
the kill; configured ask handling still applies, including codex's allow fallback.
runtime ownership enforcement requires a runner that owns the child process.

### suggestions and history

native agents can receive an initial pack suggestion when a retained catalog
advertises the analyzed command. one pack can advertise several executable names;
multiple matches are alternatives to inspect, rather than a single chosen pack.
suggestion guidance uses short names such as the `node` rule pack in conversation;
tool arguments retain the full reference. publisher and registry names distinguish
packs that share a short name.
the full registry/publisher/name reference leads to `pack_info`,
`policy_propose` and user review through `policy_apply`. a relevant
pack may still ask or deny the invocation. suggestions preserve the current
decision and activate nothing; see [catalog refresh](local-registry.md#suggestions-for-commands).

with the blocking fallback, codex explains that native approval is unavailable.
the message can offer a rule for the exact command, web search or fetched host,
or an outside folder. the agent submits that change through `policy_apply`
for your approval, then retries after activation. cli users can also use
`shield history list` and `shield rule add` directly. `shield request approve` does
not authorize a native hook retry. policy deny requires a policy change and cannot
be overridden by ordinary host approval. web searches and fetches follow web
rules; see [policy rules](policy-rules.md). git/docker effect hints do not override
allow merely because indirect effects are possible. hooks use the submitted
command and available context; they do not verify execution.
the [native run](native-run.md) flow remains a separate checked execution path.

shield mcp inspection and proposals remain available. neither a proposal nor a
diagnostic allow authorizes a command. posttooluse and claude posttoolusefailure
record available observations without output/error payloads. after you
complete an ask call, posttooluse reports the host completion and why the call
asked. completion alone does not prove individual approval. claude can inspect
`suggestion_list` after the task for eligible recurring reviews. native completions
are unlinked when the pre-call receipt is unavailable. shell exit success is
unknown unless supplied by a supported mapping.

## failure boundary and coverage

an explicit native denial prevents dispatch. the installed command also exits 2
when the shield process cannot start. a host that skips, disables, kills or times
out the hook may continue execution; installation cannot promise fail-closed
protection for those outcomes. direct same-user processes remain outside isolation.

the current implementation installs unix command hooks. windows setup refuses.
other agents have no installed native integration. native hooks cannot consume
the separate runner's stored approval grants.

claude evaluates policy before showing the prompt; shield cannot revalidate a
changed policy when that host later accepts the answer. native completion records
do not establish who approved the request. codex's exec_command hook omits workdir
and other execution options, so its reported cwd may differ from the command's
effective workdir. shield records the context the host actually supplies.

claude agent sdk read-only integration # claude agent sdk read-only integration

use `createclaudereadonlyhooks` to let a claude agent sdk host read selected
plain-text files. reads need a policy allowance or exact operator approval.
all other tools, including bash, write, edit, agent, and mcp, are denied.

the adapter uses claude agent sdk 0.3.292 and is tested on macos with its claude
code 2.1.292 process and a local provider. it has no runtime dependencies; your
host supplies the sdk. it does not install cli settings. for a normal coding
session, use [native project setup](claude-project.md).

## policy and registration

initialize the project using [the setup guide](getting-started.md). reads match
file rules against the canonical path. this rule permits `notes.txt`:

```json
{
  "id": "acme-notes",
  "decision": "allow",
  "reason": "read acme notes",
  "conditions": {
    "domain": "file",
    "action": "read",
    "sources": {"all": {"exact": {"root": "project", "path": "notes.txt"}}}
  }
}
```

declare `structured-rules-v1` and `location-v1` in the containing custom document.
see the [rule guide](policy-rules.md) for the document format.

an unmatched read returns ask: the adapter blocks it and stores a pending
request for operator review. deny blocks without creating a request. native
prompts cannot bypass these outcomes, and rules cannot enable unsupported tools.

import the adapter from this private checkout in a trusted sdk host:

```js
import { query } from '@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk';
import { createclaudereadonlyhooks } from '/path/to/canonic/packages/shield/adapters/src/modules/claude-read-only/index.mjs';

const root = '/path/to/acme';
const hooks = await createclaudereadonlyhooks({
  binary: '/path/to/canonic/packages/shield/target/release/shield',
  project: root,
  timeoutms: 5000,
});

for await (const message of query({
  prompt: 'use read to inspect /path/to/acme/notes.txt.',
  options: {
    cwd: root, hooks, settingsources: [], strictmcpconfig: true,
    mcpservers: {}, persistsession: false,
  },
})) {
  // present the message using your host application's normal interface.
}
```

replace the paths, create `notes.txt`, and activate the example rule before
running your host. its read can then proceed. without a matching allowance,
the read enters the [operator approval flow](#one-time-operator-approval).

keep the catch-all hook and transport outside agent-controlled code. do not
narrow its matcher or add input-changing hooks, settings, or plugins after it.
the example disables settings-file hooks and configured mcp servers. only the
trusted host can select the binary, project, and access classification.

## supported reads and failures

the factory fixes the project, binary, and enrollment id at startup. reenrolling
the project invalidates subsequent calls; each call otherwise reloads active policy.

a supported read must meet these limits:

- an existing regular `.txt` file, at most 65,536 bytes, containing valid utf-8
  with no nul or pdf header.
- inside the project's confirmed readable roots and outside `.shield` under
  those roots. additional `access_paths.read` or `write` roots require activation.
- no file or parent symlinks, hard links, directories, or special files.
- a cwd inside the project. optional offset and limit are integers from 1 to
  1,000,000; unknown read fields block.

shield rechecks roots, file identity, descriptor, and pathname metadata at
handoff and approval. only the checked path/window reaches `updatedinput`;
omitted window fields stay omitted.

the transport starts only the rust evaluator, using direct argv and bounded
stdin/stdout. evaluator failures, invalid replies or state, deadlines, and
cancellation return sdk deny. the deadline accepts 1–60,000 ms; the sdk callback
adds a cleanup margin. startup and filesystem calls have no hard time bound.
sdk callback timeouts block, unlike some other hook transports. do not register
`enforce-request` as a command-hook replacement.

## one-time operator approval

a blocked ask reports a stored request id. inspect it in your terminal, approve
it, then retry the identical read in the same factory and session. use `deny`
only if you want to reject the request or revoke an unused grant:

```sh
shield request list --project /path/to/acme
shield request show request_id --project /path/to/acme
shield request approve request_id --project /path/to/acme
shield request deny request_id --project /path/to/acme
```

pending requests expire after ten minutes; approval lasts five minutes.
repeating an approval returns the same grant without renewing it. revocation
is final. inspection redacts sensitive metadata and stores no file contents.

the grant binds enrollment, activation, revision, snapshot digest, canonical
path, cwd, offset/limit, file identity/metadata/content digest, session, and a
factory-owned random consumer id. the original tool-call id records provenance;
the retry has its own id. a private factory map supplies the pending reference,
so agent input cannot supply an approval flag. a changed file, policy, factory,
session, or window requires a fresh request. reconnecting also requires approval.

rust saves consumption before returning `allowed-once`; concurrent retries can
allow at most one read. lost replies, cancellation, host refusal, or missing
completion do not restore the grant. consumption records permission, not execution.

each project and factory retains at most 128 request references. terminal and
expired project records are reclaimed; unknown references and a full store
refuse requests. clearing optional history preserves authorization records,
which contain file identity, digest, and metadata, never contents.

## scope of protection

the sdk reads by pathname, not by shield's checked descriptor. external
same-user processes can replace paths after handoff; the adapter provides no
os isolation or atomic descriptor transfer.

automatic context loading and prompt `@` references are outside pretooluse.
the hook cannot filter those reads or stop unrestricted processes from invoking
the operator cli or editing state. pdfs, images, notebooks, writes, and process
execution are unsupported. native linux/windows behavior is unverified.

## decision and completion history

history is enabled by default. it records policy revision, activation, operation,
available session/tool-call ids, evaluation, and handoff result. an approved ask
keeps its original decision and links the consumed grant. unsupported tools have
no policy decision. an allowed handoff alone does not establish execution.

`posttooluse` and `posttoolusefailure` link a read completion only when project,
session, tool-call id, cwd, and path/window match the retained decision. success
records `completed`; failure records `failed`, or `cancelled` for
`is_interrupt: true`. history omits tool responses, file contents, transcripts,
error strings, and environment. unavailable version, time, and exit code stay null.

each factory keeps at most 512 correlation entries without evicting them.
additional calls remain untracked. missing entries, reused ids, mismatched input,
and purged or expired decisions leave completions unlinked. identical deliveries
appear once; changed content under one delivery id is marked conflicting.
uncorrelated callbacks can produce separate observations. missing callbacks,
including native permission or validation refusals, do not imply success.

history appends after the enforcement lock is released, retaining the original
evaluation. write failures, malformed callbacks, and transport failures report
`shield history unavailable` through `systemmessage`, without changing permission.
process death or transport loss can leave a decision without completion.

use `shield history list --project /path/to/acme` to inspect entries. the history
action in `shield policy review` controls recording and retention. see
[project history](project-review.md#request-history).

the vendor [hook reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks) and
[sdk hook guide](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks) describe the host protocol.

compiled policy cache # compiled policy cache

shield caches a compiled copy of your active policy for faster loading. it
rebuilds missing, corrupt, or incompatible entries before evaluation, without
a background service. deleting the cache does not change policy or approvals.

## prepare the cache yourself

to prepare the active policy's cache explicitly, run:

```sh
shield cache prepare
```

add `--json` for structured output. preparation does not activate file edits or
proposals. invalid saved source or an inaccessible cache directory blocks evaluation.

## find the cache

the default cache is outside the project:

| host | location |
| --- | --- |
| macos | `~/library/caches/shield` |
| linux | `$xdg_cache_home/shield`, or `~/.cache/shield` if unavailable or relative |
| windows | `%localappdata%\shield\cache` |

`shield status --json` reports the root, namespace, expected size, file
presence, and `compatibility`: `current` when this shield version can use the
saved plan, or `rebuild-required` when another version or policy built it.
`shield doctor` names a plan that needs rebuilding. on load, shield verifies the artifact's blake3 digest against the
active policy. cached regex and glob programs avoid recompiling patterns;
filesystem observations are collected for each request.

policy changes publish a new plan. cli commands and hooks load it once per
process; mcp retains evaluators for repeated diagnostics. a cache miss rebuilds
from saved source without changing activation or approvals.

on unix, directories use mode `0700` and files `0600`. native hooks protect the
cache and destructive access to its parents. windows access controls and native
linux/windows behavior are unverified.

## choose another location

choose a different root during initialization, setup or repair:

```sh
shield init --cache-dir /absolute/path/shield-cache
shield mcp setup --agent codex --cache-dir /absolute/path/shield-cache
shield cache prepare --cache-dir /absolute/path/shield-cache
```

relative paths resolve against the invoking directory. shield saves the absolute
root for hooks, sdk consumers, and mcp; tool input cannot change it. shield
creates a missing root itself. an existing root must belong to you and be
private: shield refuses one that others can read or enter (for example mode
`0755`) and does not change its permissions. run `chmod 700` on it, or name a
folder that does not exist yet. a root inside
the project gets an owned `.gitignore`. if preparation fails, shield reports the
error rather than choosing another location.

saved policy source remains in `.shield/review/sources/`. keep it and the
authority checkpoint for recovery; only the compiled cache is disposable.
cache and source storage are not automatically pruned.

developing shield # developing shield

shield is one cargo package (`canonic-shield`), library `shield`, and executable
`shield`. rust 1.99.0 is pinned with rustfmt, clippy and llvm-tools. cargo.lock
owns dependency versions; there is no root cargo workspace.

## fast iteration

from this package directory:

```sh
make dev
make test-focus filter='policy::'
# select integration tests explicitly when needed:
make test-focus filter='selected_test_name' test_target='--test integration'
```

`dev` writes an incremental build to `target/debug/shield`; run it directly to
try changes. `test-focus` uses nextest with a required substring filter and
defaults to library tests. replace the integration example's placeholder with
a real test name; nextest fails if nothing matches.

keep `target/` between iterations to reuse cargo's cache. use release builds
for performance measurements.

## source ownership

shield separates policy decisions from filesystem observations, host adapters,
and operator workflows. start with the module for the behavior you are changing:

| area | source |
| --- | --- |
| operator commands and routing | `src/cli/public.rs`, `src/cli.rs`, `src/lib.rs` |
| policy documents, selectors, requirements | `src/policy.rs`, `policy/model.rs`, `policy/rules.rs`, `policy/argument_rules.rs` |
| typed requests and resource-evidence interface | `policy/normalized.rs`, `policy/resources.rs` |
| filesystem observations and supported command effects | `src/location.rs`, `location/text.rs`, `location/node.rs` |
| shell parsing, expansion, control flow, and pid provenance | `src/shell.rs` and `shell/` |
| declared directory options | `policy/directories.rs` |
| compiled plans, indexes, and policy comparison | `policy/compiled.rs`, `policy/index.rs`, `policy/partition.rs`, `policy/profile_comparison.rs`, `policy/symbolic.rs` |
| project composition, captured source, and evaluation | `src/configuration.rs` and `configuration/` |
| shared project, policy and request inspection | `review/project.rs`, `review/history.rs`, `review/approvals.rs` |
| pack discovery, acquisition and candidate preparation | `review/packs.rs`, `review/packs/`, `review/registries.rs` |
| confirmed publication and project-file repair | `review/publication.rs`, `review/publication/projections.rs`, `review/changes/diff.rs` |
| cli questions, reviews and confirmation | `review/operator/` |
| agent configuration ownership and repair mechanics | `review/integrations.rs`, `review/integrations/`, `review/path_access.rs` |
| approval clocks and request-specific grants | `review/clock.rs`, `review/read_approval.rs`, `review/run_approval.rs` |

embedded enforcement handoff # embedded enforcement handoff

use `shield::enforcement::handoff` to embed shield in a trusted rust host.
it revalidates policy evidence and invokes your callback only for an allowed
operation. your host classifies requests and performs the operation.

for claude or codex setup, use [native project setup](claude-project.md).
for restricted sdk reads, use [claude sdk integration](claude-read-only.md).
the embedded api installs neither integration.

## integration contract

load the project's [active snapshot](runtime-activation.md), evaluate the request,
and classify it with `enforcement::agentaccess`:

| access | gate behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `ordinary` | revalidate current state; invoke the callback only for allow |
| `operator` | block approval, grants, activation, enrollment and protection disabling |
| `authorizationstatewrite` | block direct mutation of retained policy/approval/active state or its storage parents |
| `unclassified` | block unsupported or ambiguous requests |

allow rules cannot override protected or unclassified access. ask returns
`approvalrequired`, deny returns `denied`, and state or locking failures return
`runtime` with the cause. this api cannot issue or consume approval grants.

classification is the host's responsibility; `agentaccess` cannot be deserialized
from agent json. intercept every applicable tool path, including indirect writes
to state files, directories, and ancestors. the api does not inspect paths,
resolve aliases, parse vendor tools, or verify executable identity and future
shell effects. incorrect classification defeats its protection.

## handoff and failures

the callback receives the original request/evaluation while the writer lock is
held. keep it short; do not wait for process completion or acquire another review
writer lock. same-policy reactivation, foreign enrollment or corrupt state prevents
ordinary handoff. snapshot checks do not prove executable or filesystem stability.

the outer `result` reports protection failures; the inner value is the callback's
result. panic unwinding releases the lock. a lock-release error can occur after
the callback ran, so check its effects before retrying.

handoff consumes its evidence through rust ownership. callers can evaluate a new
request; consuming evidence is not a one-time approval grant. unrestricted
processes can still invoke the operator cli or write state.

## verified scope

local macos tests cover decisions, protected access, stale and corrupt state,
callback errors, and panic cleanup. doctests check ownership and reject json
access claims. host interception and request classification need their own
verification.

the embedded gate writes no audit history. the
[sdk adapter](claude-read-only.md) and [native runner](native-run.md) use separate
approval gates and record their own observations. none provides os isolation
from unrestricted same-user processes.

what is shield? # what is shield?

shield checks coding-agent requests against permissions you set for a project.
you can allow a test command, ask before a deployment, or deny changes to agent
settings. its integrations check supported claude code and codex tool calls,
and its history shows which rules decided them.

## when would i use it?

use shield to share permissions across a project, add rules for your workflow,
or investigate unexpected agent permissions. agents can suggest changes, but
you review them before they take effect.

start with the default baseline pack. you can add packs and custom rules later;
the first setup needs no handwritten policy.

## how a request gets a decision

suppose an agent submits `acme-check verify`, a fictional inspection command:

1. the integration sends shield the request and available context.
2. shield checks the **active policy**: the configuration, rules, and packs you
   last confirmed.
3. shield returns **allow**, **ask**, or **deny** and explains the matching rules.
4. the agent host handles the result using its permission settings.

an allowance for that exact command does not automatically allow
`acme-check verify --write`. arguments and working directory can be part of a
rule. a request with no deciding rule returns ask.

claude can prompt for ask. a new codex setup lets valid ask requests proceed by
default, even with a strict pack profile. see
[what happens after ask](policy-decisions.md#what-happens-after-ask).

## the pieces you configure

| term | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| policy | the rules and settings used for a project. |
| permission pack | a reusable collection of rules, such as the default baseline. |
| profile | a pack's loose, recommended, or strict decision choices. |
| custom rule | a project-specific rule, such as allowing one test command. |
| registry | a source of packs. shield includes the `main` registry. |
| integration | the hooks and mcp connection registered with an agent. |

a pack contains policy data; installing it does not install the tool it describes.
profiles select pack decisions and do not configure an agent's sandbox.

## you review permission changes

shield's terminal commands show changes before asking you to confirm. agents
can prepare proposals through mcp, the interface they use to call shield's
tools and read these guides. you approve a proposal in the host or terminal.

shield saves confirmed policy as a snapshot. manual yaml edits take effect
only after you review and activate them with `shield policy review`.

## understand the boundary

shield checks submitted requests. it cannot observe every effect of a running
command or replace your agent's sandbox. a host that skips, disables, or times
out a hook can bypass its checks.

after setup, restart and trust the agent so it loads the hooks. the
[integration guide](claude-project.md) covers supported requests and loading.
the [sdk adapter and macos runner](readme.md#integrate-with-shield) are separate
integration options.

## start with one project

follow [your first shield project](getting-started.md) to initialize policy,
connect your agent, and inspect the result. then learn
[how policy decisions work](policy-decisions.md), or go directly to
[finding a permission pack](local-registry.md#find-and-install-a-pack).

permission packs contain reusable rules for tools and workflows. registries
supply those packs; installing a pack does not install its target tool.

start with discovery below. pack authors and registry maintainers can skip to

## find and install a pack

from an initialized project, search the main registry and inspect a result:

```sh
shield pack search main/
```

`main/` searches the built-in registry without installing anything. copy a
result's full reference in place of `pack_reference`:

```sh
shield pack info pack_reference
```

read the description and profile decisions, then add the same reference:

```sh
shield pack add pack_reference --profile recommended
shield pack list
```

`pack add` reviews permission changes before confirmation. after acceptance,
`pack list` shows the selection and profile. omit `--profile` to choose interactively,
with recommended preselected.

profile decisions depend on the pack: installing one does not allow every
invocation, and strict does not change codex's ask fallback. see
[policy decisions](policy-decisions.md).

## change an installed pack

use `shield pack list` to find an installed selection. copy its selector, using the
displayed `pack:uuid` if names are ambiguous, in place of `pack_selector`:

```sh
shield pack show pack_selector
shield pack configure pack_selector
```

`show` inspects the retained selection. `configure` walks through any variable
questions and rule overrides, then reviews the change before activation. a
variable supplies a value the pack was written to accept; an override turns a
particular rule off or changes its decision. see
[pack variables and rule overrides](#pack-variables-and-rule-overrides) for
flags and local settings.

to choose another profile for that installed selection, use:

```sh
shield pack add pack_selector --profile strict
```

this preserves its retained version and pin and reviews the profile change.
profile changes use retained artifacts and can work offline.

to update unpinned selections, run:

```sh
shield pack update
```

review version and permission changes before confirming. pins are skipped;
resolution or verification failure leaves policy unchanged.

to remove a selection, use:

```sh
shield pack remove pack_selector
```

removal works offline and preserves custom rules. it refuses if a remaining
pack requires that selection; removing a root can also remove dependencies no
longer needed by another selection. inspect `shield pack list` after confirmation.
the [dependency update and removal reference](#updating-and-removing-dependency-packs)
explains these rules in detail.

## register a source

use this section when you need a local catalog or a custom https registry. you
can use the pinned `main` source without replacing it with your own registration.

choose registries explicitly, then review permission packs before installing them.
a project registration overrides the same user alias. a project default takes
precedence over the user default. the reserved `main` alias pins
`https://canonic2.github.io/shield-registry/` and the release signing key in the
binary; it installs no implicit policy. the signed main catalog is published
through github pages. a network-supplied public key cannot replace the pinned root.

```sh
shield registry add acme /path/to/local-registry
shield registry add team https://registry.example.com/ --scope user
shield registry list
shield registry list --scope user
shield registry default acme
shield pack search git
shield pack info acme/git
shield pack add acme/git --profile recommended
shield pack list
shield pack show pack:uuid
shield pack update
shield pack remove pack:uuid
shield registry remove acme
```

registry mutations ask for terminal confirmation. removing a registration
preserves installed policy and its source identity. registry aliases select
sources for discovery; installed selectors identify retained instances.
use a displayed `pack:uuid` when names are ambiguous.
that selector stays with the installed instance through updates and profile
changes. removing it retires the selector; reinstalling creates a new one.

new unversioned selections choose the highest engine-compatible stable version.
shield tries older stable releases when newer ones use an unsupported engine or
policy format. invalid digests or artifact identities stop acquisition. when you add a
new pack without `--profile`, shield asks for its profile after resolving the
release, with recommended preselected; enter keeps it. dependencies follow the
profile you choose. an exact `@version` pins that release. adding an installed selector
without a version preserves its version and pin; `--profile` changes its profile
without requiring the source to be online. update skips pinned releases and
reviews all applicable changes in one transaction. removal works offline.

## local catalog

registry maintainers define catalogs as described below. for project settings,
see [pack variables and overrides](#pack-variables-and-rule-overrides).

### suggestions for commands

claude and codex can suggest packs for commands that ask. a suggestion names
the source/publisher/pack and changes no permissions. inspect its profiles with
`pack_info`; a relevant pack may still ask or deny the invocation.
its summary includes bounded examples of declared allow, ask and deny outcomes
for each profile, with conditional rules and unmet-requirement outcomes marked.
the text preview shows recommended-profile examples. review the intended
profile's retained approval requirements alongside its allowances before
describing installation benefits. other active rules, conditions and requirements
still determine effective permissions; ask follows the host's approval or
configured fallback. omitted examples are marked in `missing`/`truncated`.

for one candidate, the agent reviews it and offers installation once per
conversation after the task, even if the command ran under codex's fallback.
it explains the scope, proposes the change, and submits `policy_apply`.
the host approval prompt is the installation question. multiple candidates
need selection first. see the [mcp walkthrough](project-mcp.md#reviewing-an-available-pack).

suggestions use the latest locally retained catalog metadata. run `shield pack search
main/` in the project to authenticate and retain the main catalog, or replace
`main` with an enrolled alias. hooks never refresh catalogs or download packs.
already installed instances and removed sources are excluded.

catalog v2 adds optional `commands`, for example
`"commands":{"acme/runtime":["node","npm","npx"]}` alongside its `packs`.
each id needs a listed stable release. lists contain 1–16 unique command basenames
(at most 64 ascii letters/digits/`._+-`, starting alphanumeric). these hints are
authenticated with the catalog, and carry relevance rather than permission.
v1 catalogs remain supported and supply no command hints. v1-only clients cannot
read v2 catalogs; upgrade clients before publishing v2. checkpoints with a command
index also require the updated client; downgrading is not supported for that state.

### catalog files

a local directory contains `catalog.json` and declarative pack artifacts:

```json
{"schema_version":1,"packs":[{"id":"acme/git","version":"0.1.0","path":"packs/git.yml","sha256":"<64-character sha-256>"}]}
```

replace the checksum placeholder with the artifact digest. artifact paths use
ascii letters, digits and `-._~/` without empty, `.` or `..` segments. an optional
`expires_at` must be a whole-second utc timestamp. an optional `sequence` is
retained like a signed catalog's: once a catalog carries one, later catalogs
must keep a sequence that never decreases. reads are confined to
the canonical enrolled directory. pack identity/version must match the catalog.
artifacts contain policy data, never installers. same-version replacement bytes
are refused for retained selections. distinct registries may supply the same pack
name; their retained identities keep those selections separate.

## custom signed https catalog

a custom https directory serves `catalog-key.pub` (64 hexadecimal characters),
`catalog.sig` (128 hexadecimal characters), `catalog.json`, and the catalog's
relative artifact paths. the key is ed25519; the detached signature covers the
exact catalog bytes. the catalog adds `registry_id`, integer `sequence` and
utc `expires_at` metadata.

enrollment verifies ordinary tls, presents the origin/key for operator review,
and retains that key and registry identity. acquisition verifies signatures,
expiry and retained monotonic sequence/digest checkpoints before using releases.
artifacts must match signed digests. redirects, unsafe paths, unsigned metadata
and source identity changes are refused. offline evaluation uses retained bytes.
this custom-source format does not supply the main registry's release trust root.

## pack dependencies

packs enable `dependencies-v1` and declare dependencies in their exact artifact bytes:

```yaml
schema_version: 1
kind: pack
id: acme/workflow
version: 1.0.0
description: acme workflow permissions
license: unlicensed
maintainers: [acme]
engines: {shield: '^0.8'}
capabilities: [structured-rules-v1, dependencies-v1]
dependencies:
  - pack: acme/git
    requirement: '^1.0'
rules: []
```

each dependency uses publisher/name and a semver requirement. it inherits the
parent's enrolled source unless `registry` names another explicitly enrolled source
identity. use the `identity` shown by `shield registry list`, rather than its alias or
the operator's default. for example:

```yaml
dependencies:
  - pack: acme/git
    requirement: '^1.0'
    registry: '<captured enrolled source identity>'
```

source or choose its url or signing key. identical pack names from different
sources stay distinct; use `pack:uuid` when names are ambiguous.

dependencies inherit the parent's profile unless a complete `profiles` mapping
selects one for each parent profile. the mapping must become at least as
restrictive from loose to strict. shared dependencies use the strongest required
profile. a directly selected dependency keeps its explicit profile and reports
a conflict if that profile is too weak. omit both `dependencies` and
`dependencies-v1` when unused; optional fields cannot be null.

### resolution and review

add and mcp pack-add proposals verify the full dependency set before review.
a new unversioned selection chooses the highest compatible stable set; existing
roots keep their versions, and exact requested versions stay pinned. cycles,
conflicts, missing releases, bad digests, or changed source identity leave
active policy unchanged.

the review lists selections, dependency/profile changes, and incoming constraints.
confirmation activates the complete candidate together. `shield pack list` and
`.shield/shield.lock` retain direct-selection flags, versions, profiles, source
identities, digests, and dependency edges. manual review rejects incomplete or
incompatible sets. promoting a dependency to a direct selection requires a
profile satisfying all its parents.

### source verification

dependencies can span enrolled local and signed https registries. resolution
uses one checked catalog snapshot per source and verifies every artifact digest.
https acquisition uses the saved origin, identity, and signing key; it never
fetches a replacement key. signature, expiry, rollback, path, size, and timeout
checks apply throughout. redirects, unknown identities, alias substitution, and
changed source bindings are refused.

captured proposals can be confirmed offline. profile changes and removal also
use saved artifacts after registry removal. dependencies accept no settings.
resolution is limited to 64 packs and bounded catalog, byte, and search budgets.
pack review runs no installers or pack code.

live in `.shield/config.local.yml` (with `rules.local.yml` and

can also turn off a shared pack for you with `disabled: true`; edit the file and

an override turns a pack rule or precondition `off` or replaces its decision;
it cannot add rules or change conditions. values and overrides are stored with

release no longer declares, and they are removed. shield asks again when an
update adds a required variable or no longer accepts the bound value. agents can
propose the same changes with the mcp `pack_configure` change.

```yaml
rules: rules.yml

      claude: acme_cloud
```

are project-only, so a pack cannot escape association through a captured request.

example, an explicit region requirement fails when the field is absent, null or
outside the allowed set:

```yaml
id: inspect-cloud
decision: allow
conditions:
  domain: mcp
  server: cloud
  tool: inspect
requirements:
  fields:
    /region: {text: {one_of: [us-east-1, eu-west-1]}}
on_unmet:
  decision: deny
```

this custom document needs `structured-rules-v1` and `requirements-v1`.

`/transport/env`, `/transport/url` and `/source` (`project` or `local`). declare

not remote credentials, oauth identity or every region used by a script.
they are derived from the selected connection; tool input cannot supply them.
there is no generic server-default inference or script analysis.

only an omitted argument may use the reviewed setting. rules read the result
under `/effective/name`; `/evidence_sources/name` identifies its source and
pointer. use this declaration only where the verified connector/tool semantics
support that precedence. unknown defaults stay absent and cannot pass a required
gate. these mappings do not invent tool arguments or modify forwarded calls.

ask follows the host's supported prompt or its confirmed ask fallback. in
particular, an allow fallback may let an ask proceed; use deny for mandatory
restrictions. native third-party server defaults remain `prompt` in generated

a pack declares `mcp_integrations` keyed by integration id. each definition has

`shield __internal run` launches a small set of macos commands under active
policy and records their outcomes. for ordinary claude or codex sessions, use
[native project setup](claude-project.md).

the runner uses literal argv, an explicit canonical cwd, and inherited standard
streams. it adds no shell or path lookup. leaf commands receive only `lc_all=c`;
git uses the settings below. start with the supported commands, then
[run an example](#run-with-active-policy).

## supported contract

| executable | arguments |
| --- | --- |
| `/bin/echo` | literal arguments, interpreted by the native echo command |
| `/usr/bin/true` | none |
| `/usr/bin/false` | none |
| `/bin/sleep` | one finite nonnegative decimal number, at most 86400 seconds |
| `/library/developer/commandlinetools/usr/bin/git` | `status`, `diff`, `diff --cached`, or `log -n n` with decimal n from 1 to 100 |

other executables, scripts, wrappers, path names, and argument forms block even
if policy allows them. linux and windows return unsupported without launching.
the runner neither enables sdk bash nor installs an agent integration.

the leaf binding requires canonical root-owned executable and dyld files on the same
read-only filesystem as `/`, without group/other write or set-id mode. the native
mach-o slice must declare exactly `/usr/lib/dyld` and
`/usr/lib/libsystem.b.dylib`, without rpaths, embedded dyld environment, custom
libraries or unrecognized load commands. file identity, metadata, filesystem
read-only state and cwd identity are rechecked at the locked launch handoff.
history retains executable and loader digests as binding evidence.

shield trusts the os and libsystem/shared cache; it does not verify apple's
boot seal or hash the full transitive cache. privileged remounts, os replacement,
and unrestricted external processes are outside its protection. cwd is passed by
pathname after revalidation, so external directory replacement remains possible.

## git inspection

git requires apple's command line tools git 2.50.1 (apple git-155) at the exact path

aliases, extra flags and other commands are unsupported.
repositories with `.git/info/attributes` are unsupported.

policy and approval match the original executable and arguments. shield adds
fixed launch arguments: no pager, fsmonitor, untracked cache, hooks, automatic

files or submodule inspection; diff disables external diff/textconv and submodule
inspection; log uses bounded one-line output without signature verification or
decoration. these controls follow the
[git diff contract](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-diff).
git has no inherited environment: lc_all=c, global/system configuration disabled,
optional locks and terminal prompts disabled, lazy fetching disabled, and explicit

are disabled; repository attributes are read from the empty sha-1 tree instead
of working/index attributes, preventing clean/process filters. diff therefore
reports raw working bytes rather than filter-normalized content. these settings
use the [git attribute-source contract](https://git-scm.com/docs/git/2.46.0).

the root-owned git executable and its root-owned, non-writable-to-other-users
parent directories are verified. its native mach-o contract permits only dyld,

remain trusted. the native image must contain the observed version marker; that
marker is a compatibility check, not independent publisher authentication.
git executable bytes are rehashed at approval issuance and launch,
along with ordinary identity checks. approvals also bind the repository directory
identity, main config and head contents, exact derived launch arguments and settings.
changing those bindings requires a fresh request.

approval does not freeze working files, the index, refs, included configuration,
or objects. git effects are not fully isolated, and privileged executable changes
or external pathname races remain possible.


## process ownership and history

the timeout defaults to 5000 ms and accepts 1..3600000 ms, including preparation.
native filesystem calls have no hard deadline. a running child gets its own process
group. sigint, sigterm and sighup are forwarded to the exact direct child and
original group; timeout sends term. a child still in that group may receive the
signal twice. after a 500 ms
grace, kill escalates even if the direct child has already exited. on ordinary
child exit, abort and guard cleanup, kill stops the direct child and remaining
original-group members, even if the direct child moved to another group. the
launcher never signals the new group it joined.
the launcher observes exit without reaping, reserves the original leader's pid
through final group cleanup, and then reaps that child. it never signals the group
after reaping. a separate 500 ms polling window requires direct-child exit and no
remaining live original-group members after kill; an observation or cleanup failure is reported as an execution
error, rather than successful completion. native inspection and reaping can block,
so these windows do not provide a hard wall-clock guarantee.
timeout exits 124; cancellation uses 128 plus the supplied signal. the direct
child's actual exit/signal remains separate from that disposition.

this covers the exact direct child and processes that remain in the original group. it does not contain
descendants that change process groups or create sessions, launch through another
host, or race group inspection with further forks. external processes joining
the group and unrestricted same-user interference are outside this ownership
contract. the supported leaf commands do not spawn descendants; wider commands
remain blocked. parent sigkill or machine failure cannot run cleanup. descendant
zombies are reaped by their parent or the os, not by shield.

the launcher holds the activation lock only through verification and spawn,
then releases it before history writes and waiting. child ownership survives
post-spawn failures; errors terminate/reap the owned child. policy changes after
launch govern future requests. inherited file descriptors and shell redirection
before shield starts belong to the invoking host, not this launch boundary.

default optional history records original policy/binding, handoff disposition,
whether spawn occurred, pid and observed exit/signal/completion. cli attribution
remains caller-declared. completion links the earlier allowed decision only while
it remains retained. no stdout/stderr is captured; literal request arguments still
follow the existing redaction contract. opt-out/purge and unavailable history do
not change execution permission or child results; failures are reported separately.
the [project history guide](project-review.md) describes inspection and settings.

native acceptance covers macos 15.7.9 with x86_64 approval fixtures. other tools,
loader configurations, and platforms are unverified. operator identity is
caller-declared.

shield in the terminal # shield in the terminal

shield guides policy changes through terminal prompts. inspection commands
print results directly. for setup, follow [your first project](getting-started.md).

## what initialization reviews

`shield init` asks for a baseline profile and agent integrations, then shows
the policy and settings changes for confirmation. recommended is preselected.
`shield init --profile strict` selects strict directly; `--no-baseline` skips the
default pack addition. existing selected baseline profiles are preserved.
codex setup preserves a saved ask fallback or defaults a new choice to allow for
every profile. the final review shows the fallback and its scope for confirmation.

the baseline comes from the pinned main registry, regardless of your default
source. its artifacts, dependencies, and catalog checkpoint activate together;
a failed download or validation leaves a new project unenrolled. use
`shield pack remove baseline` to remove it or `shield pack add main/baseline` to add it.

## controls and output

prompts appear below existing output and preserve scrollback. arrows move the
highlight; enter confirms. in multi-select lists, space marks choices and enter
continues. the footer shows the available keys.

esc goes back and keeps your answers, or cancels on the first step. ctrl-c
cancels from any step. cancellation changes nothing and exits 130. final
confirmation defaults to cancel. text fields support editing, undo, paste, and
ctrl-j for newlines; oversized input is rejected.

onboarding lists claude code and codex as independent checkboxes and preselects
those with executable clis on `path`, without starting the tools. all agents
remain available to select or deselect; aliases and tools outside `path` are not
detected. `--agent` selections bypass detection, and `--no-setup` skips agent
setup. space or a number toggles each agent; enter continues with the marked
agents. with none marked, enter skips agent setup for now. removal is offered
only by `mcp setup --remove`. `--agent claude --agent codex` selects every
registered agent directly, for `init` and `mcp setup` alike.

when enrollment is absent but generated shield host entries remain, onboarding
can reclaim entries that exactly match the current binary, project and generated
configuration. the final review shows the captured files and adoption before any
write. edited/unrecognised entries still conflict and name the configuration to
inspect; a label alone never establishes ownership.

on unix, suspension releases terminal modes; continuing restores the prompt
and draft. between prompts, signals keep their usual effect. prompts require
cursor support and enough space: redirected stdio, `term=dumb`, failed cursor
reports, and tiny terminal regions cannot confirm. set `no_color` for monochrome
output. native terminal behavior is verified on macos.

reviews list what changes: packs added (`+`), removed (`-`) or changed (`~`)
with their version, profile, rule count and short digest, custom rules, access
paths, and how command decisions change, with one example of a stricter or
broader decision. initialization and setup reviews summarize each agent's hooks,
mcp server and codex ask fallback, name the shield binary the hooks run, and
list each owned file as created, updated, unchanged or removed; shield only
changes its own entries there, so file contents are not repeated. digests show
their first 12 characters. installation and cache status are reported separately
from live interception.

errors name the failure, cause, and recovery step on stderr. recovery commands
do not run automatically. cancellation prints `cancelled; nothing changed.`
redirected stderr, `term=dumb`, and `no_color` disable ansi styling.

`--json` prints the complete result for agents and scripts: every field, full
digests and identifiers, provenance and unchanged items. json errors carry their
`code` and `message` plus `details` (the cause) and every `recovery` step.
policy-changing operations requiring confirmation refuse json/unattended
mutation, and shield has no `--yes` to accept a review unattended.
`mcp setup --dry-run --json` returns the setup review without writing. agents prepare changes as mcp proposals and request host approval with
`policy_apply`, or the operator can confirm with `shield policy review`.
`cache prepare --json` can rebuild disposable
derived data without activating source edits. native hooks, mcp and sdk
interfaces never acquire this operator ui or emit human presentation.

validating permission packs # validating permission packs

validate a pack's document, then test its decisions with example requests.
neither step executes commands or activates policy.

you need `shield` on your path and a directory for two files. no project
initialization or installation of the fictional `acme-check` tool is needed.

## prepare a small pack

save this complete document as `pack.yml` in your example directory:

```yaml
schema_version: 1
kind: pack
id: acme/inspect
version: 1.0.0
description: permit a reviewed inspection command
license: mit
maintainers: [acme]
engines: {shield: '^0.8'}
capabilities: [structured-rules-v1, argument-rules-v1]
rules:
  - id: verify
    decision: allow
    conditions:
      domain: argv
      executable: acme-check
      arguments: {kind: exact, values: [verify]}
  - id: publish
    decision: deny
    conditions:
      domain: argv
      executable: acme-check
      arguments: {kind: exact, values: [publish]}
```

this pack allows `acme-check verify`, denies `acme-check publish`, and returns
ask for other invocations. scalar decisions apply to all profiles. `engines`
declares shield 0.8 compatibility; use the range your own pack supports.

## check a document

from the directory containing `pack.yml`, run:

```sh
shield __internal validate --pack pack.yml
```

a valid document produces json and exits 0; invalid input exits 2. you can also
check a project custom-rule file with `shield __internal validate --rules path`.

## test expected decisions

save this complete fixture document as `cases.json` beside `pack.yml`:

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "cases": [
    {
      "name": "verify-is-allowed",
      "profile": "recommended",
      "argv": ["acme-check", "verify"],
      "expected": "allow"
    },
    {
      "name": "extra-option-does-not-match",
      "profile": "recommended",
      "argv": ["acme-check", "verify", "--write"],
      "expected": "ask"
    },
    {
      "name": "publish-is-denied",
      "profile": "recommended",
      "argv": ["acme-check", "publish"],
      "expected": "deny"
    }
  ]
}
```

run the fixture runner from the same directory:

```sh
shield __internal test-pack --pack pack.yml --cases cases.json
```

the json result should have `passed: true` and each case's `expected`, `actual`,
and `passed` values. exit status is 0 for a match, 1 for a mismatch, or 2 for
malformed input.

the second case checks that an extra option misses the exact allowance. change
its expectation to `allow` to see a failure, then restore `ask`. add allowed,
denied, and near-miss cases for your own pack.

### validate your own artifacts

`validate` accepts repeated `--pack` paths and an optional `--rules` document.
it checks each document's structure, capabilities, compatibility, and profile
ordering. it does not check the complete dependency set, cross-document
compatibility, or required variable bindings for activation.

`test-pack` evaluates each fixture under its selected profile. add
`--with-pack path` for companion packs under the same profile, up to 64 distinct
pack identities. `variables` binds the primary pack; companions use defaults.

## set the fixture context

fixtures use the production evaluator and fresh filesystem observations. cwd
and the default project root are the directory where you run the command;
additional access paths are not configured. add `--details` for matching rules,
requirement checks, branch outcomes, and guidance.

normalized shell fixtures test compound commands without enrolling a project.
they do not test native hooks, transport replies, or operator activation.
those checks, including extra-root behavior, need isolated enrolled projects.

### fixture fields

use `schema_version: 1` and a nonempty `cases` array with at most 1,024 entries.
each case has the following fields:

| field | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | required nonempty case name, unique in this file. |
| `profile` | required `loose`, `recommended`, or `strict`. |
| `argv` | nonempty array containing the executable followed by its arguments. use exactly one of `argv` or `input`. |
| `input` | a normalized diagnostic request, such as the shell example below. use exactly one of `argv` or `input`. |
| `expected` | required `allow`, `ask`, or `deny`. |
| `variables` | optional map binding the primary pack's variable values for this case. |

omitted variable bindings use declared defaults and are
otherwise unset. required variables without a binding or default refuse evaluator
preparation.

`input` uses the normalized diagnostic schema described in
[project mcp](project-mcp.md#diagnostic-input-and-snapshots), with an empty known

```json
  "schema_version": 1,
  "cases": [
    {
      "name": "inspection-pipeline",
      "profile": "recommended",
      "input": {
        "kind": "shell",
        "source": "git status | head -20",
        "dialect": "posix",

        "original_input": {}
```

understand policy decisions # understand policy decisions

shield returns allow, ask, or deny for a request. the agent host then handles
that decision using its integration and permission settings. for example,
codex can let an ask proceed, while its sandbox can still block an allow.

## packs, profiles, and custom rules

a permission pack contains reusable rules for a tool or workflow. installing
one adds policy data, not the tool itself.

each pack has a loose, recommended, or strict profile. the author declares the
decisions; stricter profiles cannot be more permissive. inspect those decisions
before choosing a profile.

custom rules express project-specific choices, such as allowing one command or
requiring an argument. they can tighten or relax pack decisions, but cannot
bypass protected administration checks.

## what the three decisions mean

| decision | meaning | what to check next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| allow | policy permits the supported request in the supplied context. | the host's sandbox and other permissions can still apply. |
| ask | policy requires review, or no rule decides the request. | the host's approval capability and configured ask handling determine the next step. |
| deny | policy rejects the request. | change the request or review an appropriate policy change; ordinary approval cannot override deny. |

invalid policy, unavailable required state, and protection failures block rather
than becoming an unmatched ask. unsupported tools also have their own host
handling: claude can ask for tool permission, while codex blocks unsupported
tools. a broader rule cannot add support for a tool shield cannot model.

## how rules combine

consider a custom rule allowing only `acme-check verify`, where `acme-check` is
a fictional tool you have reviewed:

| request | what to expect from that rule |
| --- | --- |
| `acme-check verify` | it matches and contributes allow. |
| `acme-check verify --write` | it misses because the argument list changed. |
| `acme-check publish` | it misses because the operation changed. |

a missed rule contributes no decision. if no other rule decides a supported
request, shield returns ask. to reject a form, match it with deny or an unmet
requirement that returns deny.

shield checks protected operations first, then project custom rules, then packs.

within custom rules and within each pack, more specific matches win. an exact
argument list ranks above an unconstrained command rule. ties resolve deny,
then ask, then allow; file order does not matter.

across packs, deny wins over ask, then allow. pack fallback rules yield to regular
rules from other packs. matching custom rules take precedence over packs, so a
custom allowance can override a pack denial. protected-state checks and denials
for other operations in the same request still apply.

for a compound shell request, an allowance for one command does not authorize
every other command or operation in it. see
[wrappers and shell commands](policy-rules.md#understand-wrappers-and-shell-commands)
for the analysis boundary.

## conditions and requirements

conditions decide whether a rule applies. requirements decide which result an
applicable rule contributes.

imagine a rule for a database command that requires `--read-only`. with that
option, the rule contributes allow. without it, an `on_unmet` branch can
contribute deny and explain how to correct the request. if you put the option
only in conditions, a request without it misses the rule entirely; another rule
or the unmatched ask fallback decides it.

this distinction matters when writing restrictions. start with the
[rule-writing guide](policy-rules.md), which shows both matching and requirement
examples.

## what happens after ask

claude's supported native requests use its permission prompt or connected sdk
permission callback. without a permission host, an unanswered ask blocks.

codex pretooluse cannot show a shield approval prompt. a new setup defaults its
ask fallback to allow for every profile; repeated setup preserves the saved
choice. with allow, valid unmatched requests and explicit ask rules can proceed.
the policy result remains ask, and history does not record that as individual
operator approval. codex's own sandbox and approvals still apply.

some requests still block: protection failures, unsupported tools, requests
requiring a rewrite, and asks fully covered by shield's codex prefix rules.
automatic ask allowance is also suspended while a confirmed setup needs repair.
see [native interception](claude-project.md) for the exact boundaries.

the separate `shield request approve` workflow grants one exact stored request for
supported sdk reads or checked native execution. it does not authorize a native
agent-hook retry. see [action approvals](project-review.md#action-approvals).

## approving a request versus changing policy

| your intent | use | effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| let a native agent request proceed after ask | the host's permission flow, where supported | handles that request under the host's approval rules. |
| approve a stored sdk read or bounded native-run request | `shield request list`, then `shield request approve request` | grants an exact retry under that workflow's limits. |
| change how future matching requests are decided | a reviewed pack or custom-rule change | publishes a new active policy. |

a policy proposal can change future permissions beyond the command that prompted
it. review its matching scope before accepting. see
[proposal review](project-mcp.md#proposals-and-operator-review).

## inspect a decision

use `shield history list`, then `shield history show entry` with an id from the list,
to see a recorded request and the rule that decided it. use `shield rule list --json`
to inspect active rules and their owners.

an agent can use `policy_evaluate` through [project mcp](project-mcp.md#diagnostic-input-and-snapshots)
to evaluate a diagnostic request. diagnostics do not execute commands, approve
them, or establish live enforcement. native hooks evaluate the submitted command
and available context; they do not attest to every effect of execution.

for unexpected results, follow [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md#the-request-was-allowed-or-blocked-unexpectedly).
